posts.title: Prompt wrappers aren't agents
posts.hook: Most "AI agents" in production are a prompt, a for-loop, and a prayer.
posts.body:
Most "AI agents" in production are a prompt, a for-loop, and a prayer.

I know because I built one that way first. It looked impressive in a demo. It fell apart the second it hit real data with edge cases.

What actually made it work: persistent memory across runs, tool selection that adapts based on prior failures, and a planning step that breaks ambiguous tasks into verifiable subtasks before execution starts.

The difference between a wrapper and an agent isn't marketing. It's whether the system can recover when step 3 of 7 fails without a human babysitting it.

My current agent pipeline runs enrichment across 4 providers, scores against ICP criteria, and routes to the right campaign. If Dropcontact times out, it falls back to PDL. If the company doesn't match firmographic filters, it logs why and moves on. No human in the loop for 95% of runs.

That's not because the prompt is clever. It's because there's actual error handling, state management, and evaluation built around it.

If your "agent" can't tell you why it made a decision, retry a failed step with a different approach, or stop itself when confidence drops below a threshold... you built a script with an LLM call in the middle.

Nothing wrong with scripts. Just don't charge agent pricing for them.
posts.cta: What's the line you draw between automation and agent in your own stack?

remixes.label: autopsy-report
remixes.hook: I shipped an "AI agent" that broke on day one. Here's the autopsy.
remixes.body:
I shipped an "AI agent" that broke on day one. Here's the autopsy.

The demo was flawless. CEO loved it. Sales was ready to pitch it. Then it hit production and started hallucinating tool calls, looping on the same failed API request, and forgetting what it had already tried.

The root cause wasn't the model. It was the architecture. I'd built a stateless prompt chain and called it an agent.

Three changes turned it into something that actually worked:

1. State that persists between runs. Not just conversation history. Structured memory of what worked, what failed, and why.

2. Tool selection with backoff. When a tool fails, the system tries a different approach instead of retrying the same broken path.

3. A planning layer that decomposes vague requests into concrete, testable steps before executing anything.

None of this is exotic. It's just software engineering applied to LLM orchestration. The problem is that most teams skip straight to "wrap a prompt in a loop" because it demos well.

Demos are not deployments. The gap between them is where agent engineering actually lives.
remixes.cta: What was the first thing that broke when you moved your AI system from demo to production?

remixes.label: taxonomy-breakdown
remixes.hook: There are four levels of AI automation. Most teams are stuck on level one and calling it level four.
remixes.body:
There are four levels of AI automation. Most teams are stuck on level one and calling it level four.

Level 1: Prompt wrapper. You send input, get output, done. No memory, no decisions, no error handling. This is 90% of what's called an "agent" today.

Level 2: Chain. Multiple prompts in sequence, maybe with some branching logic. Better, but still brittle. One bad output cascades through the whole chain.

Level 3: Reactive agent. Has tools, can decide which ones to use, recovers from some failures. This is where things start to get useful.

Level 4: Autonomous agent. Plans its own work, maintains state across sessions, learns from past failures, knows when to ask for help instead of guessing.

I spent six months thinking I was building level 4. I was building level 1 with extra steps.

The jump from 1 to 4 isn't about better prompts. It's about better architecture. Planning loops, persistent memory, failure-aware tool routing. Boring infrastructure that makes the flashy stuff actually reliable.

Stop labeling your prompt wrappers as agents. Build the infrastructure or be honest about what you're shipping.
remixes.cta: Which level would you honestly put your current AI system at?

posts.title: AI coding tools daily usage vs productivity gap
posts.hook: 71% of senior engineers use AI coding tools daily. Only 23% say it's made them more productive.
posts.body:
71% of senior engineers use AI coding tools daily. Only 23% say it's made them more productive.

That gap isn't surprising. I see the same pattern in GTM.

The tool isn't the bottleneck. The workflow around the tool is.

When I started using Claude Code, my first instinct was to use it like autocomplete. Type a comment, let it fill in code. That saved maybe 10% of my time.

What actually changed my output: treating it as a junior engineer that needs a spec. I write a CLAUDE.md with constraints, architecture decisions, and file references. I break work into tasks it can verify. I review diffs, not vibes.

Same tool. Completely different productivity curve.

The engineers saying "it doesn't help" are probably using it the way I did month one. Pasting code into a chat window and hoping for magic.

The ones getting 3x output are restructuring how they think about work. Smaller PRs. Better specs. More verification. Less time typing, more time reviewing.

AI coding tools don't make you faster at typing code. They make you faster at everything around the code, if you change how you work.

Adoption without workflow change is just a new tab you keep open.
posts.cta: Curious what workflow shift made the biggest difference for anyone actually seeing gains.

remixes.label: workflow-before-tool
remixes.hook: I tripled my output with AI coding tools. Not by switching tools. By switching how I use them.
remixes.body:
I tripled my output with AI coding tools. Not by switching tools. By switching how I use them.

For months I used Claude Code like fancy autocomplete. Write a comment, let it fill in the code. It saved maybe 10 minutes a day. I could have just typed faster.

The shift happened when I stopped thinking of it as a code generator and started treating it as a collaborator with context.

Specifically:

I started feeding it the entire file structure, not just the current file. Context about what the system does, not just what the function should return.

I started describing outcomes instead of implementations. "Make this endpoint return paginated results with cursor-based navigation" instead of "write a for loop that..."

I started using it for the tasks I hate. Test writing. Migration scripts. Boilerplate refactors. The stuff that eats hours but doesn't require creative thinking.

The 71% daily usage stat doesn't surprise me. The 23% productivity stat doesn't either. Most engineers are using these tools at the lowest leverage point. The tool works fine. The workflow is wrong.

Productivity isn't about the tool. It's about where you point it.
remixes.cta: What's the one task you've started fully delegating to AI coding tools?

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: AI coding tools might be making senior engineers slower. Not faster.
remixes.body:
AI coding tools might be making senior engineers slower. Not faster.

Sounds counterintuitive. But think about what a senior engineer's actual bottleneck is. It's not typing speed. It's not syntax lookup. It's design decisions, system reasoning, and understanding tradeoffs.

AI coding tools are optimized for the wrong bottleneck. They're incredibly fast at generating code. But a senior engineer's value isn't in code generation. It's in knowing which code NOT to write.

I've watched myself fall into this trap. Claude suggests an implementation. It's syntactically correct. It handles the happy path. I accept it. Twenty minutes later I realize it introduced a subtle concurrency issue that my gut would have caught if I'd been writing it myself.

The tool didn't save me time. It shifted my work from writing code (where I have muscle memory) to reviewing code (where I'm slower and less reliable).

The engineers seeing real productivity gains aren't using AI to replace their thinking. They're using it to handle the mechanical work they've already solved in their heads. Test generation. Boilerplate. Migration scripts. Repetitive refactors.

The leverage is in delegation of solved problems, not delegation of thinking.

posts.title: Data infrastructure is the real AI moat
posts.hook: Spent $0 on models last quarter. Spent 40+ hours building data pipelines.
posts.body:
Spent $0 on models last quarter. Spent 40+ hours building data pipelines.

That ratio tells you everything about where the real work is in AI right now.

The model is a commodity. Claude, GPT, Gemini... they all do roughly the same thing for 90% of business use cases. The difference between a system that works and one that hallucinates isn't the model. It's what you feed it.

My enrichment pipeline pulls from 6 providers, normalizes into a single schema in SQLite, deduplicates on domain + name, and scores against ICP criteria before any LLM ever sees the data. That's not glamorous work. It's plumbing.

But it means when I ask Claude to write a personalized first line, it has the prospect's actual tech stack, recent job posts, funding round, and content activity. Not a LinkedIn summary scraped 8 months ago.

Companies throwing money at fine-tuning while their CRM has 40% duplicate records and no enrichment layer are optimizing the wrong thing.

Fix your pipes first. The model will be fine.

Ten years of actual plumbing taught me this: you don't upgrade the fixtures when the supply lines are corroded. Same principle, different pipes.
posts.cta: Where are you spending more time right now, model selection or data quality?

remixes.label: garbage-in-garbage-out
remixes.hook: Your AI is only as smart as the data you feed it. And most teams are feeding it garbage.
remixes.body:
Your AI is only as smart as the data you feed it. And most teams are feeding it garbage.

I've reviewed a dozen AI implementations in the last quarter. Same pattern every time. Teams spend weeks evaluating models, running benchmarks, comparing Claude vs GPT vs Gemini. Then they feed the winner raw, unstructured, duplicated, stale data.

The model performs badly. They blame the model. Switch to a different one. Same results. Blame AI in general.

The model was never the problem.

My enrichment pipeline took 40+ hours to build. It does four things: deduplicates records, normalizes formats, fills in missing fields from multiple sources, and validates everything before it reaches the model.

That pipeline is the reason my system works. Not the model. Not the prompt. The data.

Here's the uncomfortable math. I spent $0 on model costs last quarter because I'm using Claude's subscription, not the API. But even if I'd spent $10K on API calls, the ROI would have come from the pipeline, not the model.

The teams winning with AI right now aren't picking better models. They're building better data infrastructure. Pipelines that clean, enrich, validate, and structure information before the model ever sees it.

Stop model shopping. Start pipeline building.
remixes.cta: What's the most time-consuming part of your data pipeline right now?

remixes.hook: The AI model wars are a distraction. The real competition is happening in data infrastructure nobody talks about.
remixes.body:
The AI model wars are a distraction. The real competition is happening in data infrastructure nobody talks about.

Every week there's a new benchmark. A new model that's 3% better at reasoning. A new release that supposedly changes everything. LinkedIn erupts. Twitter debates rage.

Meanwhile, the teams actually shipping AI that works are barely paying attention.

Because they learned what I learned: for 90% of business applications, the model doesn't matter. Claude, GPT, Gemini. Pick one. They all handle summarization, classification, extraction, and generation well enough.

What separates a system that delivers accurate results from one that hallucinates? The infrastructure upstream of the model.

Data collection. How are you gathering the inputs? Are they fresh or stale?
Data cleaning. Are you deduplicating, normalizing, handling edge cases?
Data enrichment. Are you combining multiple sources to fill gaps?
Data validation. Are you checking quality before it hits the model?

I spent 40+ hours building this pipeline. Zero hours debating which model to use. That ratio is intentional.

The moat in AI isn't model access. Everyone has that. The moat is proprietary data, clean pipelines, and domain-specific context that no foundation model ships with.

posts.title: AI SDRs are tanking reply rates for everyone
posts.hook: AI SDRs aren't just killing their own reply rates. They're killing yours too.
posts.body:
AI SDRs aren't just killing their own reply rates. They're killing yours too.

Every inbox is now flooded with the same AI-generated "I noticed your company is growing fast" emails. Prospects have developed antibodies. They can smell the template in the first three words.

The data backs it up. Fully automated AI outreach is pulling sub-1% reply rates. But that's not the scary part. The scary part is that well-crafted, genuinely personalized emails are also seeing declining rates because prospects now assume everything is AI slop.

So what actually works?

I run a system that's 80% automated, 20% human. The automation handles research, enrichment, ICP scoring, and draft generation. But a human reviews every email before it sends. Not for grammar. For signal.

Does this email reference something only a human would notice? A specific Reddit comment they made. A conference talk from two weeks ago. A job post that reveals a pain point.

The bar for "personalized" just went up dramatically. "I saw you're hiring for X" doesn't cut it when every AI SDR tool says the same thing.

Personalization now means showing you did work the robots didn't.
posts.cta: Anyone else seeing this decay in reply rates even on genuinely personalized sequences?

remixes.hook: Prospects have developed AI antibodies. And they're killing legitimate outreach alongside the spam.
remixes.body:
Prospects have developed AI antibodies. And they're killing legitimate outreach alongside the spam.

Here's what happened. AI SDR tools made it trivially easy to send thousands of personalized-looking emails. So everyone did. Inboxes flooded. Prospects adapted.

Now they pattern-match on the first three words. "I noticed your company..." Delete. "Congrats on the recent..." Delete. "I was impressed by..." Delete. It doesn't matter if a human actually wrote it. The template smell is enough.

This is a classic tragedy of the commons. The channel didn't die because it stopped working. It died because it worked too well for too many people at once.

The data is brutal. Fully automated AI outreach is pulling sub-1% reply rates. But here's what's worse: even carefully crafted, genuinely personalized cold emails are seeing 30-40% drops in reply rates compared to 18 months ago.

The spam poisoned the well for everyone.

What still works? Referrals. Warm intros. Content that builds trust before the ask. Community presence. Basically, anything that can't be faked by a prompt and a CSV.

The irony is thick. AI tools built to scale outreach have made outreach less scalable than ever. The only path forward is the one that was always the best path. Be genuinely relevant. Be impossible to template.

I'm competing against 50 AI SDRs hitting the same prospects. Here's how I'm winning anyway.

The average decision-maker in B2B SaaS gets 30-50 cold emails per day. Most of them are AI-generated. The prospect doesn't even read past the subject line anymore.

So I stopped trying to win the inbox. I started showing up where AI SDRs can't.

Reddit threads where my prospects ask real questions. I answer with substance, not pitches. No links. No CTAs. Just useful information from someone who clearly knows the space.

LinkedIn comments on their posts. Not "Great insight!" but actual responses that add something. This takes 5 minutes per prospect. An AI SDR can't do it because it requires genuinely understanding their specific situation.

Direct video messages that reference something specific I noticed about their stack or their hiring patterns. 60 seconds. Can't be templated. Can't be faked.

Then, when I do send the cold email, I'm not cold anymore. They've seen my name. They've read my comments. The email just connects the dots.

My reply rate on "cold" email is 14%. But it's not really cold. It's the warmest cold email in their inbox because I did the work the AI SDRs skipped.

The playbook is simple: be present where bots can't be. Then email.

38% open rate and 12% reply rate on cold email in 2026 is absolutely doable. But not the way most people are doing it.

The difference isn't copy. It's infrastructure.

Most teams are still sending from their primary domain with no warmup, no rotation, no monitoring. Then they wonder why deliverability tanks after week two.

Here's what my current setup looks like:

→ 4 sending domains, all warmed for 21+ days before any campaign touches them
→ DKIM, SPF, DMARC properly configured on every one
→ Max 30 sends per mailbox per day
→ Automated domain health checks that pause sending if reputation dips
→ Reply handling that pulls responses into Attio within minutes

That's before I write a single word of copy.

The copy matters, obviously. But I've seen perfect emails land in spam because the sender used a domain they bought yesterday. And I've seen mediocre emails get replies because they landed in primary inbox with clean reputation.

After fixing the infrastructure (4 sending domains, 3 mailboxes each, 25 sends per day max, proper authentication, dedicated IPs), the same emails with the same copy hit 38% open rates.

The copy didn't change. The subject lines didn't change. What changed was that the emails actually reached the primary inbox instead of spam.

Cold email in 2026 is an infrastructure problem disguised as a copywriting problem. Most teams are solving the wrong one.

Here's the exact cold email infrastructure getting me 38% opens and 12% replies in 2026.

No secret copy frameworks. No magic subject line formulas. Just the boring stuff nobody wants to talk about.

Domain setup: 4 sending domains, all purchased 90+ days ago. None of them are my primary business domain. Each domain has SPF, DKIM, and DMARC fully configured. All point back to my main domain with proper forwarding.

Mailbox setup: 3 mailboxes per domain. 12 total. Each warmed for 21 days minimum before any cold sends. Warmup continues even after live sends begin.

Sending limits: 25 emails per mailbox per day. No exceptions. That's 300 total sends per day across all mailboxes. Sounds low? That's the point.

Rotation: Mailboxes rotate automatically. No single mailbox sends to the same domain twice. Domains rotate weekly as primary sender.

Monitoring: Inbox placement tests every Monday. Bounce rates checked daily. Any mailbox above 3% bounce gets pulled and re-warmed. Blacklist monitoring on all domains.

First email: No links. No tracking pixels. No images. Plain text. Just a relevant observation and a question.

This setup took 3 weeks to build. It's the reason my emails land in primary inboxes while competitors hit spam. The copy matters, but only after you've earned the right to be seen.

posts.title: RevOps shouldn't own AI tool evaluation
posts.hook: RevOps is being asked to evaluate AI prospecting tools now. This is going to end badly.
posts.body:
RevOps is being asked to evaluate AI prospecting tools now. This is going to end badly.

Not because RevOps is incompetent. Because the evaluation criteria are wrong.

Most AI tool evaluations test: does it produce output? Is the UI nice? Does it integrate with our CRM?

None of those tell you if the tool actually works.

When I evaluate a prospecting tool, I run the same 200 accounts through it and through my own pipeline. Then I compare:

→ How many contacts had valid emails (verified, not "catch-all")
→ How many had accurate titles (not 18-month-old LinkedIn scrapes)
→ How many matched my ICP filters when I manually checked
→ What was the bounce rate when I actually sent to them

Most tools pass the demo. Most tools fail the comparison.

I tested one last month that returned 847 "verified" emails. Ran them through a verification API. 31% were invalid. Another 22% were catch-alls. Actual usable contacts: less than half of what the dashboard showed.

The tool looked great in the eval spreadsheet. It would have destroyed my sender reputation in production.

AI tool evaluation needs to be done by someone who understands the downstream consequences of bad data. That's usually the person sending the emails, not the person managing the CRM schema.

remixes.hook: Every AI prospecting tool demo looks amazing. That's the problem.
remixes.body:
Every AI prospecting tool demo looks amazing. That's the problem.

Vendors control the demo accounts. They cherry-pick industries with clean data. They show you the 10% of results that look magical and hide the 90% that are garbage.

I've evaluated over a dozen AI prospecting tools in the last year. Here's what I actually do before recommending any of them to clients.

First, I bring my own list. 200 accounts I already know well. If the tool can't match my existing intel on companies I've manually researched, it won't perform on companies I haven't.

Second, I run the same query three times on different days. AI tools with thin data layers produce wildly inconsistent results. Monday's "perfect ICP match" is Thursday's ghost record.

Third, I check the sourcing. Most tools scrape the same three databases and repackage them with a chat interface. If I can get the same data from Apollo for $99/month, your $500/month wrapper needs to do something Apollo can't.

The tools that survive this process are rarely the ones with the best marketing. They're the ones that can explain exactly where their data comes from and why it's different.

We keep handing AI tool decisions to the team least equipped to make them.

RevOps evaluates tools on workflow fit. Does it plug into Salesforce? Can we build reports? Does it map to our existing process?

But AI prospecting tools don't need to fit your workflow. They need to produce accurate data. And accuracy testing is a completely different skill set.

I watched a RevOps team spend three months evaluating an AI enrichment tool. They built a beautiful scorecard. Integration capabilities, pricing tiers, user permissions, API documentation. Checked every box.

Six months after buying it, sales was complaining that half the contacts bounced and the company descriptions were hallucinated.

Nobody on the evaluation team had tested data accuracy against a known baseline. They tested everything around the data without testing the data itself.

The fix isn't complicated. Pair your RevOps evaluator with someone who does hands-on prospecting. Let RevOps handle the systems fit. Let the practitioner stress-test the actual output. Two perspectives, one decision.

Tools that look great on a scorecard and tools that actually improve pipeline are often two different products.

posts.title: LinkedIn reach drop is a content quality signal
posts.hook: If your LinkedIn reach dropped 60% this year, your content didn't get worse. Everyone else's got the same.
posts.body:
If your LinkedIn reach dropped 60% this year, your content didn't get worse. Everyone else's got the same.

The platform is flooded with AI-generated posts that all sound identical. LinkedIn's algorithm is responding by deprioritizing anything that pattern-matches to generic AI output.

I track my own post performance obsessively. What still works:

→ Specific numbers from real projects (not "I helped a client 10x their pipeline")
→ Naming the actual tools and showing the workflow
→ Admitting what went wrong, not just what shipped
→ Writing like a person texting a colleague, not a keynote speaker

What's dying:

→ "5 lessons I learned about leadership" (with 5 bold headers)
→ Posts that could apply to any industry, any role, any company
→ The humble brag disguised as vulnerability
→ Anything that starts with "I've been thinking a lot about..."

The irony is that the best strategy for standing out from AI content is the same strategy that worked before AI. Be specific. Be useful. Sound like yourself.

The difference now is that generic content doesn't just underperform. It actively hurts you because the algorithm groups you with the slop.

Specificity is the new reach hack. Not because it's clever. Because everything else sounds the same.

LinkedIn's algorithm is getting better at detecting AI slop. Here's what that means for your content strategy.

I started tracking my post performance in a spreadsheet 14 months ago. Every post, every format, every topic. Impressions, engagement rate, profile visits, DMs.

The pattern is clear. Generic thought leadership posts that could have been written by anyone about anything are dying. Posts with specific details from real work are holding steady or growing.

My top-performing posts this quarter all share three traits.

They include real numbers. Not "we saw great results" but "conversion went from 2.1% to 4.7% after we changed the subject line to reference the prospect's tech stack."

They name the tool or framework specifically. Not "we used an AI tool" but "I ran this through Claude with a 50-account test set and compared against our Apollo baseline."

They admit what didn't work. Nothing triggers the "this is AI" detector faster than a post where everything goes perfectly. Real work has failures.

The irony is thick. The same AI tools flooding the platform with generic content are making authentic, specific content more valuable than ever. If you're doing real work, this algorithm shift is in your favor.

The algorithm isn't killing reach. It's filtering audiences. And if your content is specific enough to survive the filter, you're reaching a more concentrated group of people who actually care.

So yeah, your reach dropped. But if you're measuring success by impressions, you're optimizing for the wrong metric anyway. The feed is noisier than ever. The people cutting through the noise are the ones being specific enough to repel the wrong audience and attract the right one.

posts.title: Subagent orchestration is the real unlock
posts.hook: Went from 1 agent doing everything to 4 subagents doing one thing each. Output quality jumped overnight.
posts.body:
Went from 1 agent doing everything to 4 subagents doing one thing each. Output quality jumped overnight.

The pattern is simple. One agent with a massive context window trying to research, enrich, score, and write copy produces mediocre everything. Four agents with focused context windows produce good research, good enrichment, good scoring, and good copy.

My current pipeline:

→ Agent 1: Research. Pulls company data, recent news, tech stack, hiring signals
→ Agent 2: Enrichment. Finds contacts, verifies emails, maps org chart
→ Agent 3: Scoring. Runs ICP fit, intent signals, timing indicators
→ Agent 4: Copy. Writes sequences using only the scored, enriched data

Each agent gets a tight system prompt. Each one only sees the data it needs. No context pollution.

The orchestrator just passes structured output between them. If Agent 1 can't find tech stack data, Agent 4 doesn't try to fake it. The copy just doesn't mention tech stack.

This mirrors how good teams actually work. You don't ask your researcher to also write the email. You don't ask your copywriter to verify email addresses.

The mistake most people make with AI agents is treating the context window like it's unlimited. It's not. Even with 200k tokens, focus beats breadth.

Smaller scope per agent. Better output per step. Simple orchestration in between.

remixes.hook: Your AI agent is underperforming because you're asking it to hold too many things in its head at once.
remixes.body:
Your AI agent is underperforming because you're asking it to hold too many things in its head at once.

I learned this the hard way. I had one agent handling my entire prospecting pipeline. Research the company, find contacts, enrich the data, score against ICP, write the outreach. One prompt, one context window, one shot.

The output was consistently mediocre across every step. Research was shallow. Enrichment missed obvious signals. Copy was generic.

The fix wasn't better prompts. It was architecture.

I split the pipeline into four focused agents. Each one gets a narrow job and a clean context window loaded with only what it needs.

The research agent only researches. It gets the company name and returns a structured brief. Nothing else cluttering its attention.

The enrichment agent takes that brief and finds contacts, tech stack, funding data. That's its entire world.

The scoring agent evaluates the enriched data against my ICP criteria. Focused comparison, nothing else.

The copy agent gets the scored, enriched profile and writes personalized outreach. By this point, it has rich context delivered to it rather than context it had to gather itself.

Same models. Same data sources. The only change was giving each agent a single job. Output quality jumped noticeably across every step.

The parallel to human teams is obvious. You wouldn't ask one person to research, enrich, analyze, and write. You shouldn't ask one agent to either.
remixes.cta: If you're running a single-agent pipeline, try splitting just one step into its own agent. The difference is immediate.

remixes.hook: I've been running multi-agent pipelines for 8 months. Here are the three mistakes that wasted the most time.
remixes.body:
I've been running multi-agent pipelines for 8 months. Here are the three mistakes that wasted the most time.

Mistake 1: Passing too much context between agents. My first version had each agent dumping its entire output to the next one. The enrichment agent would get the research agent's full reasoning, notes, and dead ends. Noise compounded at every step. Now each agent produces a structured output format. Clean handoff, minimal noise.

Mistake 2: Not validating between steps. I assumed if the research agent said a company used Salesforce, the enrichment agent could trust that. Wrong. Early on, hallucinated tech stack data propagated through the entire pipeline and produced confidently wrong outreach. Now I have a lightweight validation step between agents that catches obvious errors.

Mistake 3: Optimizing individual agents before the pipeline worked end-to-end. I spent two weeks perfecting my research agent's prompts before I'd even connected it to the enrichment step. When I finally did, the output format didn't match what the enrichment agent expected. Get the full pipeline working with basic prompts first, then optimize each step.

The meta-lesson: multi-agent systems fail at the boundaries, not in the individual agents. Most of my debugging time is spent on what gets passed between agents, not what happens inside them.

posts.title: The boring product thesis works
posts.hook: The most boring product I've built generates the most consistent revenue.
posts.body:
The most boring product I've built generates the most consistent revenue.

It's a Reddit intent monitoring tool. It watches subreddits for buying signals, scores them, and drops qualified opportunities into a queue. No AI magic in the marketing. No "revolutionary platform." Just... monitoring and scoring.

I built it because I needed it. I was manually searching Reddit for prospects mentioning problems my clients solve. That took 2 hours a day. Now it takes 5 minutes to review the queue.

The pattern I keep seeing with solo builders who actually sustain revenue:

→ They solve their own problem first
→ The product does one thing well
→ It replaces a manual workflow they were already doing
→ The value prop fits in one sentence

Compare that to the funded startups burning cash on "AI-powered everything" platforms that require a 45-minute demo to explain.

I spent maybe 3 weeks building the core. Most of that was data pipeline work, not UI. The interface is basically a filtered list with approve/skip buttons.

No one looks at it and says "wow." But it runs every day, surfaces real opportunities, and the people using it keep using it.

Boring products that solve real workflows beat exciting products that solve imaginary ones. Every time.

remixes.body:
I stopped building what sounded impressive and started building what I was already doing manually. Revenue followed.

Every morning for months, I was opening Reddit, searching five or six subreddits for buying signals, and manually logging prospects in a spreadsheet. It took about 45 minutes a day and I never skipped it because it consistently produced warm leads.

So I automated it. Not with some grand vision of an "AI-powered intent platform." Just a script that watches subreddits, scores posts against my ICP criteria, and drops qualified opportunities into a queue I review over coffee.

No landing page with gradient backgrounds. No "revolutionary" anything. A monitoring tool that does exactly one thing.

When I showed it to three other founders, they all said the same thing: "Can I use this?" Not because the tech was impressive. Because they were doing the same manual process and hated it.

That's the signal most people miss. If you're doing something manually every day and you'd never stop doing it, other people in your space probably are too. The product isn't the automation. The product is the time back.

My flashier projects get more attention on social media. This boring monitoring tool pays the bills.
remixes.cta: What's the manual process you'd never stop doing? That's probably your next product.

remixes.hook: I never launched this product. I just started charging for it.
remixes.body:
I never launched this product. I just started charging for it.

No Product Hunt launch. No waitlist. No beta program with 500 people who never convert. I built a Reddit monitoring tool for myself, mentioned it in a few conversations, and three people asked to pay for it.

The product watches specific subreddits for buying signals. Someone posts "looking for a tool that does X" or "frustrated with Y" and the system scores it, qualifies it, and drops it into a review queue. That's it.

I charged the first three users before I had a proper login system. They got access through a shared dashboard I threw together in an afternoon. Ugly, functional, and generating revenue.

Six months later it's still the most consistent revenue source I have. Not the biggest. The most consistent. Every month, same ballpark, because the problem it solves doesn't go away.

The pattern I keep seeing with other founders: they'll spend months building something exciting, launch it with a splash, get a spike of signups, and then watch as usage flatlines because the problem they solved wasn't a daily pain point.

Boring, daily pain points make boring, daily revenue. I'll take that trade every time.

posts.title: First enterprise churn teaches more than first sale
posts.hook: Lost my first big client after 6 months. Learned more from the exit interview than from the entire engagement.
posts.body:
Lost my first big client after 6 months. Learned more from the exit interview than from the entire engagement.

They didn't churn because the product failed. They churned because their internal champion left the company and nobody else understood what the system did.

That's a documentation problem, not a product problem. But it's still my problem.

What I changed after that:

→ Every client engagement now has a "bus factor" doc. If your champion leaves, someone else can read one page and know what's running, what it costs, and what to check weekly
→ I build dashboards the client can show their boss, not just dashboards that show me the system works
→ Monthly async video walkthroughs that live in their Notion, not mine
→ Onboarding includes at least two stakeholders, never just one

The revenue hit was real. But the lesson was worth more than the contract.

Most solo founders and consultants optimize for closing. The harder skill is making yourself unchurnable. And that usually means making your work legible to people who weren't in the room when you built it.

If your product or service only makes sense when you explain it live, you have a retention time bomb.

Make the value visible without you in the room.

Your biggest client risk isn't product failure. It's the one person who understands your system leaving the company.

I call it champion dependency, and it nearly killed my first major engagement.

The system worked great. Metrics were strong. The client's VP of Revenue loved it. Then that VP took a new job, and within 60 days the new leadership team was asking, "What does this thing actually do?"

Nobody could answer. Not because the system was complex. Because all the knowledge lived in one person's head and our shared Slack channel.

I scrambled to save the account. Built documentation. Ran training sessions. Created a dashboard that showed business impact in terms a new stakeholder could immediately understand.

Too late. They'd already started evaluating replacements.

Now every engagement I run starts with what I call a "bus factor audit." Who are the people who understand this system? If any one of them left tomorrow, could the remaining team operate it? If the answer is no, that's my first deliverable: making the system survivable.

The deliverable isn't documentation for documentation's sake. It's a 30-minute onboarding flow that gets any new stakeholder to "I understand what this does and why we pay for it" without needing a walkthrough from me.

Product quality doesn't matter if institutional knowledge walks out the door.
remixes.cta: Run a bus factor audit on your biggest account this week. You might not like what you find.

After that call, I restructured my entire onboarding and documentation process. Every engagement now includes a "new stakeholder" onboarding path designed to get someone from zero to understanding in under 30 minutes.

My churn rate dropped. Not because the product improved. Because the product became survivable without its original champion.

The pattern: your churned clients have the most actionable feedback in your entire business. But you have to ask for it, and you have to be willing to hear it.

Lost my first big client after 6 months. Learned more from the exit interview than from the entire engagement.

And here's what bugs me. The product worked perfectly. Every metric was green. The system was delivering exactly what we promised. Didn't matter.

Their internal champion left the company. New leadership walked in, looked at the system, and couldn't figure out what it did. Within two months, they were evaluating replacements.

We love to talk about product-market fit like it's the only thing that matters. But there's something nobody talks about: product-org fit. Your product can be perfect and still churn if it can't survive a personnel change at the client.

The SaaS industry has a dirty secret. A massive percentage of enterprise churn has nothing to do with product quality. It happens when champions leave and nobody else was brought along for the ride.

But we don't build for that, do we? We build for the demo. For the champion's excited nod. For the signature. Then we move to the next deal and cross our fingers that our champion stays put.

After that churn, I restructured everything. Every engagement now starts with a bus factor audit and includes onboarding paths for stakeholders who weren't in the original deal. It's unglamorous work. It's also why my churn rate dropped by more than half.

platforms.linkedin:
Lost my first big client after 6 months. Learned more from the exit interview than from the entire engagement.

They didn't churn because the product failed. They churned because their internal champion left the company and nobody else understood what the system did.

That's a documentation problem, not a product problem. But it's still my problem.

What I changed after that:

→ Every client engagement now has a "bus factor" doc. If your champion leaves, someone else can read one page and know what's running, what it costs, and what to check weekly
→ I build dashboards the client can show their boss, not just dashboards that show me the system works
→ Monthly async video walkthroughs that live in their Notion, not mine
→ Onboarding includes at least two stakeholders, never just one

The revenue hit was real. But the lesson was worth more than the contract.

Most solo founders and consultants optimize for closing. The harder skill is making yourself unchurnable. And that usually means making your work legible to people who weren't in the room when you built it.

If your product or service only makes sense when you explain it live, you have a retention time bomb.

Make the value visible without you in the room.
